rule: Definite article comes AFTER the noun, not before it
notes: Kreyòl has no 'the' before the noun; the article is attached at the end of the noun phrase

rule: Use 'la' after a word ending in an oral consonant
kreyol_example: liv la; tab la; chat la
english_example: the book; the table; the cat
notes: Oral consonants: b c d f g j k l p r s t v z ch y

rule: Use 'a' after a word ending in an oral vowel
kreyol_example: papa a; bato a; kafe a
english_example: the father; the boat; the coffee
notes: Oral vowels: a e è i o ò ou

rule: Use 'an' after a word ending in a nasal vowel
kreyol_example: chen an; pen an; pon an
english_example: the dog; the bread; the bridge
notes: Nasal vowels: an en on. Words ending in -oun -in -enn -àn end in a nasal CONSONANT (see THE06)

rule: Use 'an' after an oral vowel that is preceded by a nasal consonant (m/n)
kreyol_example: zanmi an; fanmi an; lanmi an
english_example: the friend; the family; the friendship
notes: Nasal sound spreads to the article

rule: Use 'nan' after a word ending in a nasal consonant (m/n/ng)
kreyol_example: machin nan; fanm nan; moun nan
english_example: the car; the woman; the person
notes: Some speakers/regions say 'lan' instead of 'nan'

kreyol_example: liv yo; chen yo; machin yo
english_example: the books; the dogs; the cars
notes: 'yo' is invariable - it does not change with the final sound

rule: Indefinite article 'yon' (or 'on') comes BEFORE the noun
notes: 'yon' = a/an/one

rule: No article for indefinite plural or generic meaning
english_example: I bought books / I bought a book (generic)
notes: Bare noun can be generic, plural or indefinite depending on context

rule: Article goes at the very end of the whole noun phrase (after adjectives and possessors)
kreyol_example: machin wouj la; machin papa m nan
english_example: the red car; my father's car
notes: The final word of the phrase decides la/a/an/nan

rule: Article goes at the end of a relative clause attached to the noun
notes: Determiner is placed after the whole relative clause

rule: BANGS adjectives come BEFORE the noun (Beauty Age Number Goodness Size)
notes: Most other adjectives come AFTER the noun

rule: B = Beauty adjectives precede the noun
notes: bèl (beautiful/nice) ; also 'lèd' (ugly) can precede: yon lèd figi

rule: A = Age adjectives precede the noun
kreyol_example: yon jenn gason; yon vye machin
english_example: a young man; an old car
notes: jenn (young) ; vye/vyèy (old) ; nouvo (new) usually precedes too

rule: N = Number (cardinal and ordinal) precedes the noun
kreyol_example: de liv; twa moun; premye jou; dènye fwa
english_example: two books; three people; first day; last time
notes: Cardinal and ordinal numbers plus 'dènye' (last) precede

rule: G = Goodness adjectives precede the noun
kreyol_example: yon bon manje; yon move nouvèl
notes: bon (good) ; move (bad)

rule: S = Size adjectives precede the noun
kreyol_example: yon gwo kay; yon ti chat; yon gran fanmi
english_example: a big house; a little cat; a big family
notes: gwo (big) ; gran (big/tall/great) ; ti/piti (small)

rule: Multiple BANGS adjectives stack before the noun, others still follow
notes: Typical order: Beauty/Goodness > Age > Size > NOUN > other ADJ

rule: 'ti' (small) before a noun can also mean young, dear, or a small amount
notes: ti + noun often forms a compound with a special meaning (timoun = child)

rule: Most adjectives (color/nationality/shape/state) come AFTER the noun
kreyol_example: yon machin wouj; yon kay blan
english_example: a red car; a white house
notes: Exception: BANGS adjectives (see bangs category)

rule: Adjectives do not change for gender or number
kreyol_example: chen nwa yo; fanm nwa a
english_example: the black dogs; the black woman
notes: No -s plural, no feminine form

rule: No verb 'to be' between subject and adjective - the adjective acts like a verb
english_example: She is beautiful; I am tired
notes: Never say 'Li se bèl'

rule: Tense markers can go directly before an adjective
kreyol_example: Li te malad; L ap malad
english_example: He was sick; He is getting sick
notes: te + ADJ = past state ; ap + ADJ = becoming
'pase' = than

pattern: DET + pi + ADJ + NOUN or pi + ADJ + nan
kreyol_example: Se li ki pi bèl nan klas la
english_example: She is the most beautiful in the class
notes: Superlative is pi + ADJ with a context group: nan / pase tout / la

rule: Equality: osi + ADJ + pase/tankou, or menm + NOUN + ak
english_example: He is as tall as me
notes: Also: Yo gen menm laj (they are the same age)

rule: Intensifiers: trè/byen before ADJ, anpil after ADJ
kreyol_example: Li trè bèl; Li bèl anpil
notes: 'twò' = too (twò cho = too hot)

rule: Reduplication of an adjective intensifies it
notes: Also works with some verbs and adverbs

rule: 'bon' and 'move' after 'pi' are irregular in meaning
kreyol_example: Sa pi bon; Sa pi mal
english_example: That is better; That is worse
notes: pi bon = better ; pi mal/pi move = worse
Same article for all nouns regardless of gender

rule: Nouns do not change form for plural - plural is marked by 'yo' or a number
notes: Never add -s

rule: Natural gender uses separate words or 'gason'/'fi/fanm' after the noun
notes: Some pairs: frè/sè ; papa/manman ; nonm/fanm

rule: Possession: possessed NOUN + possessor NOUN (no 'of' needed)
notes: Order is the reverse of English 's

rule: Possessed noun with definite article: article goes after the possessor
notes: Article choice follows the last word (Jan -> an)

rule: Compound nouns: NOUN + NOUN, head first
kreyol_example: pye bwa; chanm dòmi; dlo kokoye
notes: Second noun describes the first
tout moun = everyone ; pèsonn/okenn moun = nobody

pattern: yon/QUANT + BANGS + NOUN + ADJ + POSS + DEM/DET + yo
kreyol_example: bèl ti kay wouj mwen sa yo
english_example: these beautiful little red houses of mine
notes: Master template for building a noun phrase
Same form for I / me / my

english_example: You are beautiful; Are you coming?
notes: Same form for you / your

rule: 3rd person singular: li (short l) - no gender
english_example: He/She/It is here; He/she is eating
notes: Same form for he / she / it / him / her / his / its
Same form for we / us / our

rule: 2nd person plural: nou (short n) - same as 'we'
english_example: All of you came / We all came
notes: Context decides we vs you-plural
Same form for they / them / their ; also impersonal 'one/people'

rule: Subject and object pronouns are the same; object goes after the verb
kreyol_example: Mwen renmen ou; Li wè m
english_example: I love you; He sees me
notes: No separate object forms

rule: Possessive: pronoun goes AFTER the noun
kreyol_example: liv mwen; kay ou; papa l
english_example: my book; your house; his/her father
notes: Short forms allowed: liv mwen -> liv m

rule: Possessive + definite article (that specific one of mine)
kreyol_example: liv mwen an; kay li a
english_example: my book (the one); his house (the one)
notes: Article choice follows the pronoun's final sound: mwen->an ; li->a ; yo->a ; ou->a ; nou->an

kreyol_example: Sa se pa m; Pa w la pi bèl
english_example: That is mine; Yours is prettier
notes: pa m/pa w/pa l/pa nou/pa yo
tèt mwen = myself ; tèt ou = yourself ; etc.
'menm' = same/even/self

rule: Short forms: use m/w/l/n/y mainly next to a vowel (before or after)
kreyol_example: M ap vini; Mwen wè l
english_example: I am coming; I see him
notes: Long form is always acceptable ; short form after a consonant is avoided in writing

rule: Impersonal 'yo' is used for passive meaning
english_example: The car was stolen (they stole the car)
notes: Kreyòl rarely uses a true passive

rule: Demonstrative 'sa a' (this/that) comes AFTER the noun
kreyol_example: liv sa a; machin sa a
notes: Kreyòl does not distinguish this vs that by default
'yo' replaces 'a'

rule: The 'a' in 'sa a' may follow the article rules (sa la / sa nan)
kreyol_example: liv sa la; moun sa nan
notes: Regional variation ; 'sa a' is the standard written form

rule: Distance can be added with 'la' or 'lòtbò a'
notes: Optional - used for emphasis

english_example: That is good; What is that?
notes: 'sa' also = what (relative): sa ou vle

rule: Demonstrative goes after adjectives and possessors
notes: Demonstrative/determiner always ends the noun phrase
'tout' can also follow a pronoun: nou tout (all of us)

rule: 'anpil' (many/a lot of) comes before the noun
notes: After a verb or ADJ it means 'a lot/very': li travay anpil

rule: 'se' links a subject to a NOUN (to be = identity)
notes: Only with nouns/pronouns - never with adjectives or places
See ADJ03

kreyol_example: Li lakay; Li nan lekòl la
english_example: He is at home; He is in the school

rule: 'ye' replaces 'se' when the predicate is moved to the front or at the end of a sentence
kreyol_example: Kouman ou ye?; Kote li ye?; Kisa sa ye?
english_example: How are you?; Where is he?; What is that?
notes: 'ye' must be sentence-final

english_example: It is me; It is true

kreyol_example: Gen yon pwoblèm; Mwen gen de pitit
english_example: There is a problem; I have two children
notes: 'genyen' is used at the end of a sentence: Wi, mwen genyen

rule: Focus/cleft: se + FOCUS + ki/... to emphasize
notes: Use 'ki' when focusing the subject

rule: Predicate cleft: se + VERB + SUBJ + VERB (repeat verb for emphasis)
notes: Emphasizes the action

rule: No marker + action verb = completed past
notes: Without a marker, action verbs usually mean past
Stative verbs: konnen, renmen, vle, genyen, bezwen, sanble, etc.

rule: te (short t) = past / past before past
notes: With a stative verb: Mwen te konnen = I knew
Can also mean near future: M ap vini demen = I will come tomorrow

english_example: We will see each other tomorrow

kreyol_example: Mwen va ale; M a ale
notes: 'a' is used after a vowel or short pronoun: m a / n a / y a

rule: pral / prale / pra = near future (going to)

notes: Also used in conditional 'would': Si m te gen lajan m t ap achte l

rule: sot / sòt / fèk / fenk = recent past (just)
kreyol_example: Li fèk rive; Mwen sot manje
english_example: He just arrived; I just ate

notes: 'konn' also means 'know how to': Li konn naje
dwe + stative = probably: Li dwe malad (he must be sick)

english_example: I finished eating / I have eaten

rule: Imperative: bare verb with no subject
notes: Add 'non' or 'tanpri' to soften: Vini non!

pattern: SUBJ + NEG + ANT + MOOD/ASP + HAB/COMP + MODAL + VERB
kreyol_example: Li pa t ap ka vini
english_example: He would not have been able to come
notes: Negation always comes first, before every marker
'te' shortens to 't' before a vowel

english_example: I am not coming / I will not come
notes: Future is negated with p ap - not 'pa va'

pattern: pa + te + ap = pa t ap

rule: Pronoun short form joins following marker
pattern: PRON + ap = m ap/w ap/l ap/n ap/y ap

rule: Verb short forms before an object or another verb
kreyol_example: M al lakay; Li vin wè m
english_example: I go home; He came to see me
notes: Full form is used at the end of a sentence: M ap ale

rule: Serial verbs: two verbs in a row describe one action
notes: Direction verbs (ale, vini, soti, monte, desann) often follow the main verb

rule: 'pa' goes BEFORE the verb and before all tense markers
kreyol_example: Mwen pa konnen; Li pa t vini
english_example: I do not know; He did not come

rule: pa ... ankò = no longer / not anymore
english_example: He does not work there anymore

notes: Double negation is normal and required
As subject: Pèsonn pa vini (nobody came)
'poko' replaces 'pa'

english_example: I do not like that at all

pattern: pa + VERB + ni X + ni Y
kreyol_example: Li pa bwè ni kafe ni te
english_example: He drinks neither coffee nor tea

rule: pa gen = there is no / do not have

english_example: No I do not want to
notes: 'non' can also go at the end for emphasis: Mwen pa konnen non

rule: Yes/no question: add 'Èske' at the start (or use rising intonation)
notes: Word order does not change

rule: Question words go at the start of the sentence
When asking about the SUBJECT, add 'ki' after the question word
kreyol_example: Ki moun ki vini?; Kisa ki rive?

english_example: What is your name? (How are you called?)

kreyol_example: Konbyen sa koute?; Konbyen pitit ou genyen?
english_example: How much does that cost?; How many children do you have?

kreyol_example: Ki liv ou li?; Ki laj ou?
english_example: Which book did you read?; How old are you?

rule: Sentence-final 'ye' when the question asks about the predicate
notes: See COP04
'ak' also = with

kreyol_example: Mwen vle ale men mwen pa ka
english_example: I want to go but I cannot

kreyol_example: Mwen pa vini paske m te malad
english_example: I did not come because I was sick

kreyol_example: Li fè nwa donk ann ale
english_example: It is dark so let's go

kreyol_example: Si ou vini m ap kontan
english_example: If you come I will be happy
notes: Hypothetical: Si m te... m t ap... (If I had... I would...)

kreyol_example: Pandan m t ap dòmi li vini
english_example: While I was sleeping he came

kreyol_example: Menmsi l ap fè lapli m ap vini
english_example: Even if it rains I will come

rule: pou = so that / in order to
kreyol_example: Mwen travay pou m ka manje
english_example: I work so that I can eat

kreyol_example: Moun ki la a se frè m
english_example: The person who is here is my brother

rule: Relative object: no word needed (ke/ki optional)
english_example: The book (that) I read is good
notes: 'ke' is optional and more formal

kreyol_example: Li di ke l ap vini
english_example: He said that he is coming
notes: Often dropped: Li di l ap vini

english_example: Since you are here help me

notes: Also used for 'to' with places: Mwen prale nan mache a

english_example: The book is on the table
The cat is under the bed

rule: anwo = above / up / on top of
bò kote / akote = beside / next to
english_example: He is sitting next to me

notes: 'de' is mostly used in fixed expressions: de tan zan tan

rule: lakay = at home / at someone's house
english_example: He is at his home; at John's house
He is inside; He is outside

rule: Places/countries usually take no preposition after motion verbs
notes: ale/vini/rive + place name with no 'to'

rule: mwen -> m ; ou -> w ; li -> l ; nou -> n ; yo -> y
notes: Used mostly next to vowels and in speech

rule: Short object pronoun attaches after a verb ending in a vowel
kreyol_example: Mwen wè l; Li rele m
english_example: I see him; He called me

rule: nan -> n or lan in fast speech
notes: Write 'nan' in standard spelling

rule: Every letter is pronounced - no silent letters
notes: Spelling is phonetic (official 1979 orthography)
Accent changes the word
ò is open like 'law' ; o is closed like 'go'

rule: an, en, on are nasal vowels; use 'àn' when a and n are pronounced separately
notes: Grave accent on 'à' marks non-nasal 'a' before 'n'

rule: ch = sh sound ; j = zh sound ; g is always hard ; s is always s

notes: 'w' is its consonant form
